A safety net fund for victims of misconduct in the finance sector is facing a $170m shortfall after the recent collapse of several major firms.

It is the latest blow for victims of the failed First Guardian Master Fund and the Shield Master Fund collapsed, with 11,000 people losing an estimated $1.1bn.

The Compensation Scheme of Last Resort (CSLR) was set up following the banking royal commission to pay back anyone who lost money due to financial misconduct if the companies responsible went broke.

The federal government was expecting to handle 912 claims for the upcoming financial year, but the collapse of First Guardian, Shield and Dixon Advisory has pushed that up to 1567 claims.

The CSLR, which is funded by levies on the finance sector, needs more than $190m to pay out all victims but only has $20m.

The Super Members Council said on Thursday the shortfall again exposed the need for stronger protections.

“A tsunami of unpaid compensation orders is now flooding the scheme,” chief executive Misha Schubert said.

“This highlights the absolute urgency of the need for stronger laws to protect consumers from these types of devastating harms in the first place, and an equally urgent need to enable super funds to deliver more safe, trusted financial advice to their own members.”

She said that only “large-scale consumer safety reforms that comprehensively lift the bar on consumer safety will stop continuous flooding of the scheme”.

Stockbrokers and Investment Advisers Association chief executive Maria Lykouras agreed on “the unsustainability of the compensation scheme” but said rules needed to be tightened for claimants.

“The CSLR must be fundamentally redesigned,” she said.

“Now that the scheme is in its third year of operation, its shortcomings are obvious.

“Alarmingly, the estimate shows that the fees incurred to run the scheme in FY 2027 including AFCA fees exceed the entire personal financial advice subsector cap of $20 million.”

She went on to take aim at counterfactual claims, or losses that cover unrealised profits, pointing out that some 80 per cent of CSLR payouts to Dixon Advisory complainants were counterfactual losses.

“A total of $83,497,000 in compensation is estimated to be paid to Dixon Advisory complainants in FY 27,” Ms Lykouras said.

“If ‘but for’ losses are a large component of this amount, this highlights the extraordinary burden that losses based on foregone profits place on the scheme.”

She added that the CSLR was “never intended to underwrite investment risk or pay complainants hypothetical ‘but for’ gains”.

Originally published as Financial misconduct victim fund missing $170m amid claim spike
